title: Grove's Freezer can cancel the issuer's queued Timelock changes while Grove's SubProxy executes them
content:
The Timelock that holds `OWNER_ROLE` over a Tokenized Treasury Instance is operated by the credit token issuer, but its three internal roles are split across parties. The issuer holds `PROPOSER_ROLE` (specified per Instance, per A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.1.2.1). The `EXECUTOR_ROLE`, which runs a queued operation once the delay elapses, "is held by the Grove SubProxy Account" (A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.1.2.7). The `CANCELLER_ROLE`, which kills a queued operation before execution, "is held by the Freezer Multisig across all Tokenized Treasury Instances, and additionally by the credit token issuer's address that holds the Timelock's `PROPOSER_ROLE`" (A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.1.2.8).

This converts a standard timelock into a **mutual-consent mechanism**. The issuer can queue a change to a contract Grove has money in, but cannot enact it — enactment requires Grove's SubProxy — and Grove's emergency responders can cancel it outright during the delay window.

The timelock delay stops being merely a notice period and becomes a **veto window**. Its purpose is not just to let observers see a change coming; it is to give a specific named party time to stop it.

Giving Cancel to the Freezer Multisig rather than to the SubProxy is consistent with the subtractive-emergency-power pattern: cancellation is purely negative, so it belongs with the fast 2-of-5 responder, while execution — an affirmative act — sits with the slower governance-controlled SubProxy.

For an allocator, this is the mechanism that makes a third-party-owned vault tolerable at size. Grove's protection against adverse changes to an instrument it does not own is procedural rather than contractual: it holds one half of the enactment path and a share of the abort switch.
description: Across all Tokenized Treasury Instances the Freezer Multisig holds Canceller and the SubProxy holds Executor on the issuer-operated Timelock, so the issuer proposes but cannot unilaterally enact.
